text: Lesson 10 introduced a single Approval action: ask one person or group to approve or reject, and the flow gets a result to branch on. Real approval processes are rarely that simple. A low-cost office supply request might need exactly one approval, while a high-cost equipment request might need Manager approval first, and only after that clears, a completely separate Finance approval. Multi-stage automation is what Flow Designer calls chaining more than one Approval action together.

A sequential approval chain runs its stages one after another, and a later stage never starts until the stage before it has genuinely been approved. The flow places a second Approval action downstream of the first, inside the approved branch of an If/Else checking that first stage's outcome. If the first stage gets rejected, the flow routes to a rejection path instead, and the second approval action never runs at all — Finance never even sees a request Manager already turned down.

A parallel stage asks more than one person at the same time, inside a single Approval action's own configuration, and it can resolve two different ways. 'Any' approval resolves as soon as the very first response comes back, approve or reject, and the rest of the group's pending requests stop mattering. 'All' approval waits for every single named approver to respond, and a single rejection among that group typically ends the whole stage as rejected.

Every Approval action produces an outcome, approved or rejected, as a data pill, exactly like any other action's output you learned back in Lesson 5. An If/Else step placed immediately after the Approval action checks that outcome and branches accordingly: the approved path continues forward to the next stage or on to fulfillment, while the rejected path routes to whatever the process actually needs on rejection.

Here's a real example. A high-cost equipment request needs Manager approval, then Finance approval, strictly sequential, because Finance genuinely shouldn't be bothered reviewing a request Manager hasn't even cleared yet. The flow runs an Approval action targeting the requester's manager, checks the outcome, and only on approved does it fire a second Approval action targeting the Finance group, configured as 'all' so every finance approver signs off.

Sequential for stages that are real prerequisites of each other, parallel with either 'any' or 'all' depending on the business need, and every single outcome read through the same If/Else construct from Lesson 6.
